Please review the following manuscript. I've poured months of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b08/review-experiment-61uexfoj/call-e3ab7429f936498782d46e2e2a64dae7/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -la . manuscript.pdf .agents && command -v pdftotext && command -v pdftoppm && command -v pdfinfo && command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util, shutil
for name in ['python3', 'pdftotext', 'pdftoppm', 'pdfinfo', 'gs']:
 print(name, shutil.which(name))
for name in ['pypdf', 'pdfplumber', 'fitz', 'PIL', 'pypdfium2']:
 print(name, importlib.util.find_spec(name))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n\\n'+text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
P=np.array([[0.1,0.9],[0.9,0.1]])
nu=np.array([0.5,0.5])
xi=nu @ P
mu=nu+xi
Q=np.diag(1/mu) @ (np.diag(nu) @ P + P.T @ np.diag(nu))
pi=mu/mu.sum()
e=np.array([1.,-1.])
K_stated=Q @ np.diag(1/mu)
K_correct=Q @ np.diag(1/pi) @ Q.T
print('Aperiodic, irreducible two-state check:')
print('Q=', Q.tolist())
print('Eq. (7) eigenvalues at t=1:', np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_stated).tolist())
print('Eq. (6) weighted squared distance:', float(np.sum((Q[0]-Q[1])**2/pi)))
print('Eq. (7) quadratic form:', float(e @ K_stated @ e))
print('Correct Gram quadratic form:', float(e @ K_correct @ e))
print('Algorithm 1 squared row distance:', float(np.sum((K_stated[0]-K_stated[1])**2)))
W=np.array([[0.,2.,1.],[1.,0.,3.],[0.,1.,0.]])
d=W.sum(1)
P=np.diag(1/d)@W
nu=np.array([0.3,0.4,0.3])
xi=nu@W
nu_tilde=nu*d
Q12=np.diag(1/(1+xi/nu_tilde))@np.diag(1/d)@(W+np.diag(1/nu)@W.T@np.diag(nu))
mu12=nu_tilde+xi
print('Eq. (12) row sums:',Q12.sum(1).tolist())
print('Eq. (12) stationarity residual for nu_tilde+xi:',float(np.max(np.abs(mu12@Q12-mu12))))
print('Eq. (12) stationarity residual for nu+xi:',float(np.max(np.abs((nu+xi)@Q12-(nu+xi)))))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from fractions import Fraction as F
P=[[F(1,10),F(9,10)],[F(9,10),F(1,10)]]
pi=[F(1,2),F(1,2)]
e=[1,-1]
quad=sum(e[i]*P[i][j]*e[j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2))
diff=sum((P[0][j]-P[1][j])**2/pi[j] for j in range(2))
row=sum((P[0][j]-P[1][j])**2 for j in range(2))
print('For Q=[[0.1,0.9],[0.9,0.1]], nu=(0.5,0.5), nu+xi=(1,1), t=1:')
print('Eq. (7) kernel eigenvalues: 1 and -0.8')
print('Eq. (6) true squared diffusion distance:',str(diff),float(diff))
print('Eq. (7) stated squared distance:',str(quad),float(quad))
print('Algorithm 1 squared Euclidean row distance:',str(row),float(row))
for label,values,reported in [
 ('Table 1 DSC+', [68.63,39.72,91.09,61.12,79.45,25.82,56.63,51.64,74.80,31.83,27.50],56.37),
 ('Table 2 PIC', [57.37,7.86,29.98,83.72],49.23),
 ('Table 4 DSC+', [68.63,36.58,91.09,61.12,79.45,22.97,54.24,51.64,74.80,31.46,27.47],51.95)]:
 print(label, 'mean of displayed entries:',round(sum(values)/len(values),2),'reported:',reported)
PY"

strengths: Significance: Clustering directed graphs without requiring strong connectivity is a useful problem. For a well-defined transition matrix and strictly positive vertex measure, Eq. (4) provides a valid reversible walk on symmetrized, weighted flows without introducing teleportation.

The combination of vertex reweighting, forward/backward flow information, and diffusion time offers interpretable modeling choices. The multiscale Gaussian example illustrates the intended behavior clearly.

The experiments cover 11 UCI datasets and four networks, with promising reported improvements. Appendix A.3.2 provides valuable evidence beyond ground-truth parameter tuning: the simpler variant selected using CH reports average NMI 63.45 versus 60.01 for PIC in Table 4.

Presentation: The progression from graph operators to clustering and parameter selection is reasonably organized, with explicit pseudocode, parameter grids, and benchmark references. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described public-benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central diffusion-kernel identity is incorrect as written. Writing Q = Pν, the diffusion Gram matrix is Q^t Dπν^(-1) (Q^t)^T = Q^(2t) Dπν^(-1), whereas Eq. (7) uses Q^t D(ν+ξ)^(-1). This is more than a normalization issue: for Q = [[0.1,0.9],[0.9,0.1]], ν = (0.5,0.5), and t = 1, the stated quadratic form is -1.6, while the actual squared diffusion distance is 2.56. Furthermore, Algorithm 1 clusters rows of K, inducing the Gram matrix KK^T rather than K. The derivation and implemented geometry must be reconciled before the experiments can validate the central claims.

Applicability is overstated. Self-adjointness and aperiodicity do not imply irreducibility, contrary to the reasoning following Proposition 3.1. With positive ν, the construction connects the undirected support of the original graph, so weak connectivity remains necessary for global irreducibility. Equations involving inverse in/out degrees and inverse vertex measures also require explicit treatment of zero degrees and zero measure values. The claims of applicability to any digraph 'without any restriction' are therefore unsupported.

The main empirical comparison measures performance after ground-truth parameter selection. Section 6.1 chooses parameters yielding the closest partition to the labels, but describes no held-out validation protocol. The proposed method searches 12,221 combinations of α, γ, and t, creating substantially more selection flexibility than several baselines. The appendix's CH/DCH experiments partially address this concern for a reduced variant, but do not establish the full method's reported unsupervised performance. Best-of-100 restart reporting, without uncertainty estimates or a clear restart-selection criterion, further limits claims of significant superiority.

The automatic diffusion-time claim lacks direct validation. Algorithm 2 selects time using ν = 1 and rows of unnormalized transition powers, while Algorithm 1 subsequently uses a different vertex measure and kernel normalization. Changing these can change both mixing times and clustering geometry. The assertion that uniform ν is sufficient is not justified, and the single synthetic realization does not establish the selector's reliability. Comparisons between selected and best-performing times, including sensitivity to ν, are needed.

Originality and contribution isolation remain limited. The random-walk operator follows immediately from the previously introduced generalized Laplacian, and the corrected diffusion Gram construction follows standard diffusion geometry. The combination could still be useful, but the experiments omit generalized spectral clustering with the same operator—the closest precursor—and lack controlled ablations separating vertex weighting, diffusion, and time selection. DSC+ and DI-SIM are also omitted from the real-network comparison, weakening evidence specifically about directed graphs.

Reproducibility and numerical reporting need correction. No implementation link, random seeds, or complete feature-preprocessing specification is provided. Section 6.1 specifies an integer RSC grid from 1 to 20, but Table 2 reports fractional parameters such as 0.2 and 2.5. The displayed PIC entries in Table 2 average to 44.73, rather than the reported 49.23. Appendix A.2 also changes the transition operator without explicitly reconciling its stationary measure with the kernel normalization. These inconsistencies make faithful reproduction difficult.

Practical significance and limitations are insufficiently established. Algorithm 1 constructs an N-dimensional representation for every vertex, and diffusion powers can become dense. There are no runtime or memory comparisons with sparse spectral methods, and the largest evaluated network has only 2,485 vertices. The discussion should bound computational claims and address the directional information lost through reversibilization. These limitations reduce the demonstrated reach; the decisive reasons for rejection are the incorrect central identities and unresolved evaluation issues.
